lead: A chip is tested many times: on the wafer, after packaging, after it is soldered to a board, and inside the finished product. Each level uses a different fixture, catches different faults and costs more per failure than the one before. Chip-level and system-level test plans what to test where, and how to reach the cores buried inside a system-on-chip (SoC) through a small number of pins.
prereq: You need: test cost and the test steps from 6.1, scan from 6.4 and boundary scan from 6.5.

items: Wafer sort. A probe card touches every die. DC checks, scan and memory tests run at modest speed; bad die are mapped and never packaged.
Package (final) test. The packaged part runs the full test at speed, hot and cold. It catches bonding and assembly faults and speed failures the probe could not measure.
Board test. After soldering: solder bridges, open tracks, missing or rotated parts. In-circuit test and boundary scan do this work.
System test. The finished product boots and runs its software and interfaces. It tests the whole product, so it is the last place an escape can be caught.

blocks.text: The cost of finding a fault rises at each level; a common rule of thumb is about ten times per level. A fault found at wafer sort costs one die. Found at system test, it costs a die, a package, a board, other parts and hours of debug.

where C is the wafer-sort plus packaging cost per good die shipped (₹), N the die on the wafer, c<sub>w</sub> the wafer-sort cost per die, N<sub>p</sub> the die that reach packaging, c<sub>p</sub> the packaging cost per die and N<sub>g</sub> the good die shipped.

items: Known-good die (KGD). A die sold bare for a multi-chip module or a 3D stack must be proved good before bonding, because one bad die scraps the whole module.
Burn-in. Hours at raised voltage and temperature turn weak parts into dead ones before shipping.
Multi-site test. Testing many die at once lowers cw but needs more tester channels.

blocks.text: An SoC is assembled from cores: processor, memory controller, USB, DSP, analog blocks, often from different vendors. The issues in testing such a chip are set by its size and its pins. Verification has billions of states to cover, so the design is checked block by block and then as a system; test must be planned at RTL, because adding it after layout costs area and timing. Each core arrives with its own test set and cannot be reached from the pins directly; the chip has far fewer pins than all its cores' test ports added up; and testing every core at once may draw more power than the package can take.

items: Core wrapper. A ring of cells around a core. In test mode it isolates the core, applies its vectors and captures its responses. IEEE 1500 standardises the wrapper and its serial control.
Test access mechanism (TAM). On-chip wires that carry test data from chip pins to the wrappers. A TAM of width w moves w bits per clock.
Test scheduling. Decides which cores are tested together, within the TAM width and the power limit.
Control. One IEEE 1149.1 TAP (6.5) usually sets the modes of all the wrappers.

blocks.where: where T is a core's test time in clocks, P its number of patterns and ℓ the length of its longest wrapper scan chain. Giving a core more TAM wires shortens ℓ only if its scan cells can be split into more chains.

sections.h3: Board test, system test and test coding

blocks.text: In-circuit test (ICT) presses a bed of nails onto the board's nets and measures each part: fast, but the fixture is costly and fits one board. A flying probe moves a few needles over the board: no fixture, slower, good for prototypes. Boundary scan replaces most nails on dense boards, and its port also loads chip tests and programs flash.

Test coding, as some syllabi call it, is how a test is written down for the tester and kept small. The test program is a file of vectors plus timing (when each input changes and when each output is strobed), written in a tester language or a standard format such as STIL (IEEE 1450), so a pattern made by an ATPG tool runs on any tester. The scan data is then coded to fit the tester memory. Most bits of an ATPG vector are don't-cares, so they can be filled to make long runs of 0s and the runs sent as short codes, or an on-chip decompressor can expand a few tester channels into hundreds of short internal chains, with a compactor squeezing the outputs back.

examples.question: A wafer holds 1000 die, of which 200 are defective. Wafer sort costs ₹6 per die and catches 90 % of the bad die. Packaging costs ₹80 per die. Final test removes any bad die left, so 800 good die ship in both plans. Find the wafer-sort plus packaging cost per good die (a) without wafer sort and (b) with it.
steps: (b) Wafer sort: 1000 × ₹6 = ₹6,000. Bad die caught: 0.90 × 200 = 180, so 1000 − 180 = 820 die are packaged.
Saving = ₹100.00 − ₹89.50 = ₹10.50 per good die, 10.5 %. Check: the 180 die not packaged save 180 × ₹80 = ₹14,400, the sort costs ₹6,000, and the difference ₹8,400 ÷ 800 = ₹10.50.
examples.answer: ₹100.00 per good die without wafer sort and ₹89.50 with it, a saving of ₹10.50 (10.5 %).

examples.question: An SoC has a TAM 8 wires wide. Core A has 4 internal scan chains of 200 cells and 500 patterns; core B has 4 chains of 150 cells and 800 patterns. Neither core can use more than 4 TAM wires. Find the total test time (a) testing A and then B, each given all 8 wires, and (b) testing both together on 4 wires each. The scan clock is 100 MHz.
steps: (a) One after the other: 8 wires do not help, since each core has only 4 chains. Total = 100,700 + 120,950 = 221,650 clocks = 2.217 ms.
(b) Together on 4 + 4 wires: total = the longer core = 120,950 clocks = 1.210 ms.
Saving = 221,650 − 120,950 = 100,700 clocks, 45.4 %. If the cores could use the full width, the serial plan would be as fast; sharing pays here because each core uses only half the TAM.
examples.answer: 2.217 ms when the cores are tested one after the other and 1.210 ms when they share the TAM 4 + 4, a 45.4 % saving, as long as the power limit allows both cores to run together.

traps: Dividing by all die instead of good die shipped. Cost per good die uses the good parts that leave the line.
Thinking wafer sort replaces final test. Bonding faults and speed failures appear only after assembly.
Mixing up scan (chip-internal DFT) and boundary scan (pins and board wiring). They use different cells and catch different faults.
Assuming a wider TAM always speeds a core. A core with fixed internal chains cannot use more wires than it has chains.
Testing every core at once without checking power. Scan switching in all cores together can exceed the package's power limit.

quiz.q: Name the four test levels a chip passes through, in order.
quiz.a: Wafer sort, package (final) test, board test, system test.

quiz.q: What is a known-good die and why is it needed?
quiz.a: A bare die proved good before it is bonded into a multi-chip module or stack; one bad die would scrap the whole module.

quiz.q: List three issues that make testing an SoC built from cores harder than testing a single block.
quiz.a: Each core's test ports are buried and need a wrapper and a TAM; the chip has far fewer pins than the cores' test ports added up; testing all cores at once can exceed the power limit. Verification is also split, block by block and then as a system.

quiz.q: What does an IEEE 1500 core wrapper do?
quiz.a: It isolates the core in test mode, applies test data to the core's inputs, captures its outputs, and is set up through a serial control port, so a core can be tested from outside with few pins.

quiz.q: A wafer has 2000 die and 300 are defective. Wafer sort costs ₹5 per die and catches 80 % of the bad die; packaging costs ₹100 per die. Find the cost per good die with and without wafer sort.
A core has 6,000 scan cells and 400 patterns. Find its test time in clocks on a 4-wire TAM and on an 8-wire TAM, if the cells can be split evenly into as many chains as wires.
A chip passes wafer sort and package test but fails at board test. What fault is most likely, and which tool finds it?
quiz.a: A board fault: a solder bridge, an open track, or a missing or rotated part, since the chip itself passed. Boundary scan with EXTEST, or in-circuit test, locates it.

beyond: Not for the exam. Test scheduling is an optimisation problem: tools pack cores into a fixed TAM width under a power budget with integer programming and heuristics. Chiplets and 3D stacks need known-good die and new standards for test through the stack (IEEE 1838), and cars ask chips to test themselves in the field. Search 'IEEE 1500 wrapper', 'test scheduling SoC' and 'IEEE 1838'.
